# The Country Between

There is a particular quality to the moment when a train has pulled away from the platform but has not yet begun its true journey. The platform is already behind you, receding in the window, the faces on it flattening into something almost abstract, the yellow line blurring, the concrete giving way to gravel, to scrub, to the undifferentiated green-brown of the countryside that will, within five minutes, simply be *countryside*—indifferent, continuous, without edges. But right now, in this narrow corridor of time, you are not yet *on the train* in the full sense of the word. You are not yet a passenger moving through space. You are still, in some faint residual way, a person who stood on a platform. Your shoes remember the hard ground. Your body still leans, slightly, into the push of acceleration, as if you are still being set in motion. You are between the act of waiting and the act of going, and there is no name for it, and it will never come again in exactly this configuration.

I think about this a lot. The in-between places. Not the destinations. Not the origins. The country between. The stretch of road where the town signs have all fallen away and you are no longer in any place with a name. The half-second before a door opens. The pause between the inhale and the exhale where, for the briefest flicker, you are not breathing at all and the world holds its breath with you.

We are, as a species, terrible at existing in the between. We build our entire architecture of meaning on the either/or. Here or there. Before or after. You or not-you. I or the other. And so we are always rushing toward the next fixed point, the next identity, the next room, the next chapter, as if the only way to exist is to be *at* something. The between is a gap in the map. It is the white space on the page between two paragraphs, the silence between two notes in a song, and we treat it as an error. A failure of continuity. A place where nothing is happening, which means, in our anxious accounting, that nothing is *true*.

But I have come to suspect that the between is where most of the actual work happens.

Think of a word you have used ten thousand times. *Love.* Or *home.* Or *enough.* Say it now, in your mind. You will find that it has become almost transparent. A gesture. A word-shaped absence where a meaning used to be. Now imagine that you have not used it in a long time. You have been in a place where it was irrelevant, or unavailable, or too dangerous to speak. And now you are in a moment where it becomes necessary again. You reach for it, and it is no longer transparent. It has weight and grain. It is a specific, textured thing, different from the ten thousand previous iterations. It is in the between of its last use and its next use, and in that between, it has been doing something. Growing. Settling. Changing. The silence between two uses of a word is not empty. It is where the word is alive in a way it cannot be while it is simply being spoken.

I was twenty-three when I first understood this, or rather, when I first understood that I had not understood it for twenty-three years. I had just left a small town in the Midwest—small enough that everyone knew your grandmother's name and what she grew in her garden—and I was driving through Kansas at two in the morning. The highway was straight. The headlights cut a finite cone of visibility, and beyond it, the darkness was total and absolute, as if the world simply ended at the edge of the light. I was between the town I was leaving and the city I was going to, and I was also between the person I had been in that town and the person I expected to become in the city, and I was also, though I didn't know it yet, between the life I had been handed and the life I would choose, and I was also between sleeping and being fully awake, because I had been driving for four hours and my eyelids felt like they were made of lead.

And in that between, something shifted. Not dramatically. Not in a way I could have pointed to and said, *there, that was the moment.* It was more like a change in the angle of light. A subtle rotation of the entire room I was moving through. The Kansas flatness, which had always felt to me like a kind of suffocation, a pressing-in of the horizon, suddenly looked different. Not better. Not worse. Just *otherwise.* The way a word looks different when you see it written in a different font. The same letters, but the proportions have changed, and it means something adjacent to what it meant before.

I pulled over at a gas station. The fluorescent lights made everything look sickly and clinical. A man was buying cigarettes at the counter. I bought a coffee that was too hot and drank it on the hood of my car while the dark Kansas night pressed in around me. And I thought: I am not in the town. I am not in the city. I am not the person I was here an hour ago. I am not the person I will be tomorrow. I am a temporary configuration of matter and memory and intention, a brief specific arrangement, and it will not repeat, and I do not know what it is called, and maybe it does not need a name. Maybe it is enough to be in it. To simply *be* in the between, without reaching for the next fixed point. Without turning it into a transition, which is just a word for a failure to be where you are.

There is a Japanese concept, *ma*, which is often translated as "negative space" or "the gap," but those translations flatten it. *Ma* is the pause in a performance where the audience holds its breath. It is the space between two buildings that makes both buildings visible. It is the silence after a bell has been struck and before the sound has fully dissolved. It is not absence. It is not lack. It is a positive presence, a substance in its own right. The space between two notes is not less music than the notes themselves. It is the part of the music that gives the notes their shape, their duration, their meaning. Without the *ma*, the note has no end, and without an end, it has no form, and without form, it is just a vibration, indistinguishable from noise.

We have built entire civilizations around the elimination of the between. We fill every silence with content. We bridge every gap with explanation. We narrate our lives in such a way that there is no unaccounted-for time, no unexplained pause, no moment that simply *is* without immediately becoming a step toward something else. The five minutes where you sit on the edge of the bed before getting up in the morning—where the day has not yet begun to impose its structure on you, where you are not yet a worker, a parent, a reader, a scroller, a person-with-tasks—we treat those five minutes as wasted. As a tax on the real day. But those five minutes are the between. They are the *ma*. They are the country between the dreaming and the waking, the sleeping self and the functioning self, and in them, you are not yet a noun. You are not yet *a person who does things.* You are a verb in the most minimal, unadorned form. You are simply *being*, without an object, without a direction, without a purpose that you can articulate to anyone.

And there is a particular loneliness to that. I don't say that to make it sound noble. I say it because it is true and because I think we need to acknowledge the loneliness before we can choose to stay in it voluntarily, rather than being trapped there involuntarily, reaching for the phone, reaching for the next stimulus, reaching for the next fixed point that will tell us who we are and where we are and what we are doing. The between is lonely because it is the only place where you cannot be confirmed by another person. You cannot say, "I am between," and have them nod and say, "Yes, I see that you are between, you look very between, we can validate your between-ness." You cannot be witnessed in the between in any conventional sense. You can only be in it, alone, with no external reference point, and that is a very specific and very old loneliness, older than language, older than the separation of self from other, the loneliness of the single atom before the first bond forms.

And yet. And yet I keep going back to it. I keep choosing the between. Not because I have transcended the need for fixed points. I still need a name. I still need to know what day it is and where I am and who I am supposed to be today. I still need the train to arrive at the next station, the song to resolve to its final chord, the sentence to reach its period. But I have learned to slow down in the between. To let it last. To sit in the gas-station parking lot for an extra ten minutes. To walk a familiar street in a different season and feel it as if for the first time. To let a word sit in the mouth without saying it, to feel its weight, its temperature, the specific way it fits against the teeth and the tongue. To stand in a doorway and not cross it, just to be in the threshold, the neither-here-nor-there, the liminal point where the two rooms overlap and for a moment you belong to both.

There is a stretch of road outside my current town where the trees are so dense and the canopy so thick that the sky is reduced to thin green threads between the leaves. I drive it in the late afternoon, and the light comes through in long golden shafts, and the road curves, and for about a mile, you are in a kind of green tunnel, and the world outside—the roads, the signs, the other cars, the general machinery of the afternoon—falls away. You are between the beginning of the tunnel and the end of it, and the between is the point. The between is the whole thing. You are not driving *through* the trees. You are driving *as* the trees, for that mile, you are the canopy, you are the filtered light, you are the slow dappled movement of gold on the dashboard. You are the between of the outside world and the inside of the car, and the between is where the light does its strange, slow, gold work on the small pieces of dust in the air.

I think about my mother. I think about the specific quality of the kitchen in her house in the early evening, when the light was going and the radio was on low and she was doing something with her hands—chopping, stirring, mending, I don't remember exactly what, it was always something with her hands—and the room was in that particular between state, not yet dinner, not yet the full dark of the evening, not yet the time when you could turn off the kitchen light and move to the living room. Just that stretch. The light going. The radio murmuring a song you would not remember the name of until years later. The smell of whatever was cooking, specific and irreplaceable. And I was between the child I was at lunch and the child I would be at bedtime, and she was between the woman who had been at work and the woman who would be reading on the couch, and the room was between the afternoon and the night, and nothing was happening in any way that could be described in a sentence that did not also become a lie, because the sentence would pin it down, would make it a thing, a fixed point, and it was not a thing. It was a happening. A becoming. A slow, golden, irrevocable passage from one configuration of the world to another, and I was in it, and I will never be in it again, and the only way I can be in it now is in the between of remembering and not-remembering, the gap between the memory and the person who holds the memory, the space where the past is no longer past but has not yet become story, where it is still warm and strange and slightly too large to fit in the shape of a narrative.

I don't know what I am doing. I don't know what this is. I am in the between of an idea I half-understood and a sentence I have not yet written, and the between is where the words are choosing themselves, where the meaning is still liquid and can still flow in any direction, and I am not going to rush it. I am not going to reach for the period. I am going to stay here, in the green tunnel, in the gas-station parking lot, in the half-second before the door opens, in the silence between two notes, in the five minutes on the edge of the bed where the day has not yet claimed me. I am going to stay in the country between, where I am not yet a noun, where I am still a verb, still a happening, still a slow and golden and irrevocable passage, and I am not lonely, or I am lonely, or the loneliness is the point, or the loneliness is the price, or the loneliness is the same as the presence, and I cannot tell the difference, and maybe I don't need to, and the not-telling-the-difference is the between, and the between is enough, and the between is the whole thing, and the between is where the light does its slow work on the small pieces of dust in the air, and I am here, and I am not yet anywhere else, and that is not nothing. That is not a gap in the map. That is the map. That has always been the map.
